topic: Confirmation bias: you only see what you already believe
title: Your Brain Hides Evidence You Disagree With
voiceover: You're not seeing all the evidence. Here's why. In 1960, psychologist Peter Wason gave people three numbers: 2, 4, 6. Their job was to guess the hidden rule. Many guessed 'add two each time,' then tested only numbers that fit, like 8, 10, 12. All of them got a yes. The real rule was simply any increasing numbers. Many people never tested something that could prove them wrong, like 5, 4, 3. That's confirmation bias: searching for, favoring, and remembering information that supports what you already believe. Try this: before an important decision, ask 'what would prove me wrong?' Then actually go look for it. Sources that disagree with you aren't enemies. They're free error-checking. Tomorrow: why unfinished tasks keep nagging at the back of your mind.

description: Your brain naturally seeks out information that agrees with what you already believe. Peter Wason's classic 2-4-6 task shows how people test ideas in ways that can only confirm them. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Wason (1960), 'On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task', Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology.
accuracy_note: Wason's task is a classic demonstration of seeking confirming evidence; it is a simplified model of real-world belief formation. Confirmation bias is robust but not absolute: people can be nudged to look for disconfirming evidence.
